artists.biography:
Mother Earth were an acid jazz outfit based in London, formed by long time Acid Jazz associate Bunny and basically comprising Matt Deighton on guitar and vocals, Bryn Barklam on Hammond organ, Chris White on drums and Neil Corcoran on bass. Shauna Green was the lead singer on the first album. Prior to their debut live performance where they played alongside another debutant band Jamiroquai, they started out as a studio project in 1991 with Paul Weller (on "Almost Grown"), James Taylor of the James Taylor Quartet and Simon Bartholomew from the Brand New Heavies as contributors.
In total they released three studio albums and one live album. After they disbanded in 1996, two retrospective albums were released in 2001 and 2004.

perplexity.description:
Stoned Woman is the debut album by London-based acid jazz ensemble Mother Earth, released in 1992 on Acid Jazz Records. The album showcases the band's fusion of soul-rock, jazz-rock, and acid jazz influences, featuring the vocal work of Shauna Green alongside the instrumental prowess of Matt Deighton on guitar, Bryn Barklam on Hammond organ, Chris White on drums, and Neil Corcoran on bass. The project emerged from a collaborative studio initiative that included contributions from notable musicians such as Paul Weller, James Taylor of the James Taylor Quartet, and Simon Bartholomew from the Brand New Heavies, establishing the band's connections within the broader acid jazz movement of the early 1990s.

The album represents Mother Earth's entry into a vibrant period of British acid jazz, arriving at a time when the genre was gaining significant cultural traction. Stoned Woman established the sonic template that would define the band's approach across their subsequent releases, blending organic instrumentation with the groovy, funk-influenced sensibilities characteristic of the Acid Jazz label's roster. The album's nine-track composition demonstrates the band's ability to balance intricate arrangements with accessible songwriting, drawing from funk, soul, and jazz traditions while maintaining the contemporary edge that defined early 1990s acid jazz.

While specific critical reception data is limited, Stoned Woman served as the foundation for Mother Earth's three-album run throughout the 1990s before their disbandment in 1996. The album's legacy was acknowledged through retrospective compilations released in 2001 and 2004, indicating the band's sustained relevance within acid jazz circles and their contribution to a pivotal moment in British jazz-funk history.
